# The last night

On Saturday, 7 November, I finished my last night shift.

It ran from nine in the evening until half past seven in the morning, in majors. I’ve worked nights for fourteen years: my first was as an SHO in 2012. On Monday, I move to a days-only rota.

I expected to feel triumphant, perhaps. Instead, I drove home on Sunday morning down the London Road with the sun coming up and the Radio 4 shipping forecast playing on catch-up, and realised I would not see that light from this side again.

I don’t mean I’ll never be awake at sunrise. I mean that particular view: the city still quiet, the day arriving while you’re heading home, carrying the odd feeling of having been somewhere most people weren’t. I thought I’d be ready to leave it. I’m relieved to be leaving it. Both things are true.

Fourteen years is long enough for nights to get into your habits, your friendships, even your sense of what a working day is. They give you a different version of the department. There are fewer managers around and, somehow, less room for pretending. At night, people tend to say what they mean. They notice who needs help. There is more honesty, and often more kindness.

People imagine nights as a string of adrenaline-filled emergencies. There are emergencies, of course. But much of the work is quieter than that: thinking clearly when you’re tired, explaining something for the third time, finding a way to stay kind at five in the morning when you’re empty. The impressive thing is rarely a dramatic intervention. More often it’s the person who keeps showing up for the next patient with patience still to give.

There are small rituals, too. At four in the morning, somebody makes toast in the staff room. Nobody admits to starting it. The toast appears, and people drift towards it as if called by a bell they can’t quite hear. I don’t know when it became a tradition or who maintains it. I only know that, at four, toast tastes like a small act of faith in the shift continuing.

My first winter on nights, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary because I couldn’t remember whether I’d given a patient the second dose of a medication. I had. I checked, and I had. But I can still see the frost on the windscreen and remember the fear of not being certain. It wasn’t a grand crisis. It was one tired person in a cold car park trying to hold all the details in her head. I have thought about that version of myself often since. I wish I could tell her that uncertainty gets easier to sit with, though I’m not sure it ever disappears.

Last winter, around three in the morning, an older gentleman held my hand and told me I had his daughter’s hands. I won’t say more about him. He went home three days later. I’ve carried that moment with me—not because it made the work simple or beautiful, but because it was so ordinary and so strange: a brief kindness between people who had only just met.

Then there are all the things nights took, often without anyone meaning for them to. I missed both my nieces’ naming ceremonies over video because of work. My sister never once complained. She was in Bangalore, and I watched from a screen, grateful to be included and aware that being included wasn’t quite the same as being there. I don’t blame the nights for every absence; life is made of choices and circumstances that don’t always line up neatly. Still, I missed those mornings. I wish I could have held them.

My body has been keeping its own record. My knees are less keen than they were, sleep doesn’t come as easily, and my GP has made it clear that my blood pressure is not a joke anymore. So the move to days is partly a decision I’m grateful to have been able to make. It’s also a change I didn’t expect to mourn.

Our charge nurse, Folasade, has worked nights for twenty-two years. She still beats me up the stairs. I have no explanation for this, except that perhaps it is unwise to assume a person’s knees are a reliable guide to their speed.

I’ve watched Folasade do what good night-shift nurses do: keep a steady eye on the room, on the team, and on the people who need us. There’s no fuss in it. Just attention, experience and the kind of practical care that can make a difficult shift feel possible. If nights have a character, she is part of it.

I keep wanting to write about this, and finding myself at one of two dead ends: a eulogy or a complaint about the NHS. Neither feels right. I’ve written enough about the pressures and frustrations. They matter, but they aren’t the whole story. And nights aren’t something I want to praise so extravagantly that I forget what they cost.

The honest version is less tidy. Nights gave me colleagues who became friends, a different kind of closeness with the people I worked beside, and memories I didn’t know I was collecting. They gave me the four o’clock toast, the frost on the windscreen, the quiet drive home. They gave me work that asked for attention and kindness, again and again.

They also took sleep, ordinary weekends and mornings with family. They wore me down in ways I’m only now learning to measure. I’m relieved to be finished. I feel like a traitor for being relieved.

That feeling may take a while to leave. Maybe it doesn’t have to. I can be grateful for the years and glad they’re over. I can miss the strange light on the way home without wanting to spend another night under it.

On Monday, the rota changes. Somewhere in the department, at four in the morning, someone will make toast. Nobody will admit to starting it. And Folasade, I suspect, will still beat everyone up the stairs.
